title: Extra Example B
summary: Find MK in the right-angled ΔLMK, then add KN to get MN.
alt: Extra Example B: In ΔLMN, ∠M = 90°. K lies on MN such that LK = 17 cm, LM = 8 cm and KN = 9 cm. Find the length of MN.

hyp.label: Hypotenuse
hyp.text: The side opposite the right angle. It is always the longest side.

legA.label: Shorter side 1
legA.text: One of the two sides that meet at the right angle.

legB.label: Shorter side 2
legB.text: The other side that meets at the right angle.

steps.title: The question
steps.narration: In **ΔLMN**, **∠M = 90°**. **K** lies on **MN** such that **LK = 17 cm**, **LM = 8 cm** and **KN = 9 cm**. We have to find **MN**.

steps.title: Spot the right angle
steps.narration: In ΔLMK, **∠M = 90°**, so the **hypotenuse** is the side opposite it: **LK**. The other two sides meet at the right angle.

steps.title: Pythagoras' theorem
steps.narration: **Pythagoras' theorem**: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{LK^2} &= \role{legA}{LM^2} + \role{legB}{MK^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Make the unknown the subject
steps.narration: We want a **shorter side**, so subtract the known square from the hypotenuse square.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{LK^2} &= \role{legA}{LM^2} + \role{legB}{MK^2} \\ \role{legB}{MK^2} &= \role{hyp}{LK^2} - \role{legA}{LM^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Substitute the lengths
steps.narration: Replace each side by its length.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{LK^2} &= \role{legA}{LM^2} + \role{legB}{MK^2} \\ \role{legB}{MK^2} &= \role{hyp}{LK^2} - \role{legA}{LM^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{17^2} - \role{legA}{8^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Square root
steps.narration: Take the square root of both sides (a length is positive).\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{LK^2} &= \role{legA}{LM^2} + \role{legB}{MK^2} \\ \role{legB}{MK^2} &= \role{hyp}{LK^2} - \role{legA}{LM^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{17^2} - \role{legA}{8^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{289} - \role{legA}{64} \\ &= \role{legB}{225} \\ \role{legB}{MK} &= \sqrt{225} = 15\ \text{cm}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Add KN
steps.narration: **MN** is made of **MK** and **KN**.\[\begin{aligned}MN &= MK + KN \\ &= 15 + 9 \\ &= \role{ans}{24\ \text{cm}}\end{aligned}\]

formulas.title: Pythagoras' theorem
formulas.text: In a right-angled triangle, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

formulas.title: Finding the hypotenuse
formulas.text: Add the two squares, then take the square root.

formulas.title: Finding a shorter side
formulas.text: Subtract the known shorter side's square from the hypotenuse's square, then take the square root.

challenges.title: Now you try
challenges.prompt: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse **13 cm** and one shorter side **5 cm**. Find the other shorter side.

takeaways: Pythagoras' theorem works only in **right-angled** triangles — mark every right angle in the figure first.
Split the figure into right-angled triangles and solve them **one at a time**; each answer feeds the next triangle.
Keep a few extra decimal places in the middle of a calculation and round only the **final** answer (3 s.f.).

notes.title: Exam tip
notes.text: Always begin with a line such as "In ΔABC, ∠C = 90°. Using Pythagoras' Theorem," — it shows which triangle and which right angle you are using.
